$comment: Illustrative machine-readable CBOM profile for PQC migration planning. DERIVED: this profile extends the interface disclosure baseline under the composition rules on the Profile page. It inherits every baseline rule, tightens one, and adds six per-interface rules, one group rule with nine members and one product-level rule. Its own rules are numbered from I1, G1 and P1 in its own space: an id is local to the profile that declares them and is cited as 'pqc-migration#I1'. See decision 0011. Extension is monotonic, so a CBOM conforming to this profile also conforms to the baseline. DRAFT v0.7: this file is the baseline depth of the PQC migration family proposed in decision 0022. It sits in drafts/ until its examples are updated; it pins the draft Interface Disclosure Baseline v0.8 beside it, which carries module validation (interface-disclosure#I10, #I11) and key wrapping on storage (interface-disclosure#I12). The use-case page docs/use-cases/pqc-migration.html is the target model for this file.
title: PQC Migration Readiness (Example)

objective.$comment: C1. A derived profile states its own consumer and decision; it does not inherit the base's, because the whole reason to derive is that the decision differs. The same applies to decisionOptions: the base's consumer chooses whether to accept a disclosure, and this one chooses what to do about an interface.
objective.consumer: An operator planning a post-quantum migration across an estate of products it did not build.
objective.decision: For each interface a product exposes: whether it can be made quantum-safe, what enabling it requires, what enabling it costs in interoperability, and where the capability is not yet available, what is preventing it and who controls that.
decisionOptions: enable the capability on the deployed product
schedule a software update to obtain it
replace the product, where no update path reaches it
accept the interface as it stands and revisit at the next review
escalate to the supplier, where the blocker is theirs to clear

scope.$comment: C11. Narrows the base's accepted lifecycle stages, which is a tightening and therefore permitted; widening would be a relaxation and the validator rejects it. 'intended' is excluded because a migration plan built on cryptography a producer intends to implement is a plan built on an intention. The other three describe something that exists: implemented in the shipped product, configured in a deployment, or observed running. Where a producer can only report an intention, the fact belongs to the capability group G1, not to a lifecycle stage. 'cryptographicPurposes' declares which purposes this profile takes in scope, meaning those that owe the whole member set G1.1 to G1.9. Every other purpose that applies to the interface still owes G1.6 (status), G1.7 (blocker, where not available) and G1.9 (validated mode, where available), which is what keeps a staged profile from becoming a floor. 'encryption' stays a deferred purpose (decision 0010). 'key-wrapping' is taken in scope by the extended depth, not here. See decision 0010.

appliesTo.$comment: Must lie within the base profile's range. A derived profile may narrow the accepted carrier versions and may not widen them.

$inherited: The disclosure model and the requirement keywords are inherited from the base and are deliberately not restated. Restating an inherited block would override the base's value silently, so a later change to the base, such as a new marker prefix, would not reach this profile and every marker would stop being recognised without an error. Only appliesTo is restated, because narrowing the carrier range is a real choice and the validator checks that a restated range does not widen the base's. The module-validation vocabulary is likewise inherited from the base and not restated.
$commentCryptographicPurpose: The jobs cryptography does at an interface, each migrating on its own timetable. A purpose is not an operation: CycloneDX 'cryptoFunctions' already records sign/verify, and one sign/verify covers both a TLS certificate signature and a firmware signature, which migrate a decade apart and call for different work. Only the purpose carries a timetable. Entries qualify under the four-part test in decision 0010: declarable at the boundary, independently migratable, actionable, and not an ingredient of another purpose. That test excludes certificate path validation, which migrates when entity authentication does, and hashing, which is an ingredient of several purposes. 'randomness' is deliberately absent and left open in decision 0010. Note that a purpose is not a partition of algorithms: AES-GCM serves 'encryption' and 'data-integrity' at once, so an asset may appear under several purposes. 'key-wrapping' replaces the earlier 'key-protection' (decision 0022 records the rename, as it changes decision 0010's list).
$commentValidatedMode: Whether a capability that exists can be used while the module runs in its validated mode. The common case this records: a provider ships ML-KEM before the validation covering it is issued, so the capability is available in the product and unavailable to an operator obliged to run in validated mode. The attribute states the fact. Whether validated mode is required is the operator's policy and is not recorded. The module validation it is read against (moduleValidationScheme, moduleValidationRef) is stated by the baseline, as interface-disclosure#I10 and #I11.
$commentInheritance: Added in v0.7 (decision 0022, K9), reworded in the revision that aligned this file with the use-case page. Rules are evaluated on effective values. Four attributes and the capability group describe the implementation rather than the boundary: moduleValidationScheme and moduleValidationRef (rules of the baseline), providerLocation, coexistence, and each capabilityByPurpose entry. A document may state them once on the implementation that provides an interface; the interface inherits them and states a value only where it differs. Precedence is per attribute, and per purpose for the group: an interface's entry for one purpose replaces the provider's entry for that purpose as a whole, so a status never travels without its blocker. The entry carries enablementMethod, minimumProductVersion, negotiationStrategy, negotiationControl and integrationConstraints as well as the status, so all of them are inherited together and overridden together; they are no longer separate interface-level attributes. Attributes that describe the boundary are never inherited: interfaceType, endpointRoles, lifecycleStage, and the algorithm attributes. How the providing implementation is identified is the mapping's business.

overrides.note: Tightened by removing withholdability. The base already requires implementationPurl at MUST and accepts a 'withheld' marker in place of a value. Migration sequencing depends on knowing which library implements an interface, so this profile removes that option and requires the value itself. Level is restated as MUST for readability and is unchanged from the base.

productRules.description: Product identifies at least one cryptographic provider
productRules.note: This profile's only product-level rule, and therefore P1 in its own space. The baseline's P1 to P4 are inherited and keep their own ids: the two are told apart as 'pqc-migration#P1' and 'interface-disclosure#P1', which is what a report and a conformance claim print. The coverage rule this profile used to carry has moved into the baseline and is now inherited. See decision 0011.

interfaceRules.note: Guarded in v0.7 to match the base's rule for the present-state attribute: not required of a storage interface, which has no protocol, key exchange or peer authentication. Its capability counterpart on storage is I6. See decision 0022.

Guarded in v0.7 to match the base's rule for the present-state attribute: not required of a storage interface, which has no protocol, key exchange or peer authentication. Its capability counterpart on storage is I6. See decision 0022.

Guarded in v0.7 to match the base's rule for the present-state attribute: not required of a storage interface, which has no protocol, key exchange or peer authentication. Its capability counterpart on storage is I6. See decision 0022.
Was I6 in the v0.6 file and in the first v0.7 draft; renumbered to close the gap left by the removal of the interface-level enablement rules (decision 0011 permits it while nothing is released).
Was I7 in the v0.6 file and in the first v0.7 draft; renumbered like I4.

Added in v0.7. On a storage interface: the wrapping algorithms the storage path can be configured to use, or 'none'. Capability counterpart of the base's keyWrapping (interface-disclosure#I12), in the same relation as keyExchangeSupported (I2) to keyExchange and authenticationSupported (I3) to authentication, and for the same reason: the methodology's 'Supported' suffix denotes what an interface is able to use, and the baseline, being an inventory profile, may not require a forward-looking attribute (C12). Declaring storage interfaces at all is required only at the extended depth; once one is declared, it is described in full at every depth. The use-case page lists the same pair (interface-disclosure#I12 keyWrapping and pqc-migration#I6 keyWrappingSupported). They are kept apart so that the baseline stays an inventory profile (check C12; decision 0022).

groupRules.$comment: Settles Q27. Readiness was a single value per interface, which cannot express the ordinary position: key agreement done, identity proof not yet. It is now a repeated group keyed by cryptographic purpose, so an interface states what it can do for each job its cryptography does. The blocker's guard is evaluated inside a group member rather than across the interface, which is what makes it evaluable again: it asks about the status of one purpose rather than about the interface as a whole. Nine members: the facts that differ from one purpose to another on the same interface (route, version, negotiation, constraints) and the status, blocker, roadmap and validated-mode facts. See decision 0010 and decision 0022.

keyApplicability.$comment: PROPOSED FORMAT ADDITION 1, not implemented by validate_cbom.py, profile.schema.json or check_profile.py (decision 0022, point 8). Which purpose keys an interface owes. Each guard has the shape of requiredWhen and is evaluated with the same condition_holds against the interface, not against the entry, since the entry does not see interfaceType. A key whose guard is not met is reported 'n/a', not as missing. 'otherKeys' applies to every key without its own entry in 'perKey'. A derived profile may remove a guard but not add or narrow one (decision 0014). Until the evaluator reads this property it requires an entry for every key in the vocabulary, and every interface fails G1 for the keys that do not apply to it.

groupRules.description: Every cryptographic purpose that applies to the interface has an entry stating its capability
groupRules.note: A storage interface owes only the key-wrapping entry; any other interface owes the other six. Within an entry, a purpose in scope (scope.cryptographicPurposes) owes all nine members. Every other purpose owes G1.6, G1.7 where the status is not 'available' and G1.9 where it is. That is close to the cheapest obligation a profile can impose, and it is what stops a staged profile becoming a permanent floor: a supplier cannot conform while behaving as though authentication does not exist, and a buyer sees the long-lead blockers in the first document rather than the third. A missing entry is reported against the group (pqc-migration#G1) and names the purpose; a member such as G1.6 fails only inside an entry that exists. Cascade: G1.7 is guarded 'notEquals available', which holds when capabilityStatus is absent, so omitting G1.6 inside an entry fails G1.7 as well (see decision 0022, absent-attribute cascade).

members.note: Was interface-level I4 in the first v0.7 draft. Stated per purpose because the route differs: a TLS key exchange may arrive with a runtime update while the signature on the same interface is not available at all. 'inScopeOnly' is PROPOSED FORMAT ADDITION 2 (see G1.5).

Was interface-level I5 in the first v0.7 draft. Conditional within the entry: applies only where this purpose's capability is enabled by a software update. The guard reads the entry's own enablementMethod, so it has one value to test.

New in v0.7. How the interface selects an algorithm with its peers: static, exclusive, preference-order, client-controlled or dynamic. Governs algorithm selection; negotiationControl (G1.4) says whether the operator can change it.

Was interface-level I8 in the first v0.7 draft. A leading word (configurable, fixed or policy-controlled) followed by the configuration mechanism as prose. Whether the integrator can customise algorithm selection, reorder priorities or refuse fallbacks, in particular whether post-quantum can be required and a classical fallback refused. Whether the far end can be pinned or forced is sometimes contractual; a producer may decline to publish it. Open: whether the mechanism gets its own field.

Was interface-level I9 in the first v0.7 draft. Known effects of enabling the capability: size limits, intermediaries, performance. PROPOSED FORMAT ADDITION 2, not implemented by validate_cbom.py (decision 0022, point 8): 'inScopeOnly' on G1.1 to G1.5 extends the validator's existing skip. Today check_group_rule drops only MAY members for a purpose outside scope; with the flag it also drops a flagged member, so a deferred purpose owes G1.6, G1.7 and G1.9 only. G1.8 is a MAY and is already skipped. Until the evaluator reads the flag it requires G1.1 to G1.5 for every purpose.
Was G1.1 in the first v0.7 draft and in the v0.6 file.

Was G1.2 in the first v0.7 draft and in the v0.6 file. Conditional within the entry. Applies wherever this purpose's capability is not already available. The 'certification' value rests on interface-disclosure#I10.
Was G1.3 in the first v0.7 draft and in the v0.6 file.

Was G1.4 in the first v0.7 draft. Conditional within the entry: applies where this purpose's capability is available. SHOULD at this depth so the baseline stays reachable; the extended depth tightens it to MUST and keeps the guard, so it is a conditional MUST there. A producer declaring moduleValidationScheme 'none' answers 'no-validated-mode'. That agreement is not checkable by the evaluator, which evaluates each rule on its own.

exclusions.item: A date on which an interface will gain a capability
exclusions.reason: Interfaces do not gain capability independently of one another, and a date offered where the blocker is an unfinished standard is not one the vendor can keep. The profile records capabilityStatus, blockedBy and roadmapRef instead. See decision 0007.

exclusions.item: Any judgement as to whether an interface is quantum-safe
exclusions.reason: Inherited from the baseline. The profile requires the algorithm sets an interface uses and supports, and leaves the judgement to external versioned policy. See decision 0002.

exclusions.item: Internal migration plans, engineering schedules, and unreleased design detail
exclusions.reason: Outside the black-box boundary. Anything the profile requires must be declarable at an interface or stated as a property of the shipped product.

exclusions.item: encryptionSupported, the counterpart of the inherited encryption attribute
exclusions.reason: The profile adds a Supported form for key exchange, authentication, key wrapping and protocol version, and deliberately not for bulk encryption. A quantum computer degrades symmetric encryption rather than defeating it, so the migration is a key-length change within the same algorithm family and does not constrain sequencing in the way a key exchange or signature change does. A consumer needing it reads the inherited encryption attribute and the product's documentation.

exclusions.item: Per-algorithm capability status within a single interface
exclusions.reason: Still excluded, but for a different reason than before. Status is now stated per cryptographic purpose (G1), which is the granularity at which timetables actually differ; per algorithm is finer than any planner acts on, and breaks where one algorithm serves two purposes. What was deferred here as Q27 is settled by decision 0010. The algorithms an interface can negotiate are carried by the interface-level Supported attributes (I2, I3, I6), not by a member of G1.

exclusions.item: A per-algorithm flag stating whether an algorithm is approved or quantum-safe
exclusions.reason: Both are derived. Approval follows from the module's validation reference (interface-disclosure#I11) and its security policy; quantum safety follows from external versioned policy. The profile records the reference and the algorithm names. See decision 0002. Where an available capability cannot be used in validated mode, G1.9 states that fact per purpose.

artifacts.$comment: C9. The Keycloak pair replaces the gateway pair, which does not state module validation. The conforming document conforms only once the evaluator reads the attributes added in v0.7 and the explicit 'none' values (see the extended profile's '$pendingTooling'), and the two proposed group-rule format additions (keyApplicability, inScopeOnly); the verdicts were checked with those gaps patched outside the repository. The non-conforming document fails the group rule pqc-migration#G1 and nothing else: sto-realm-keys has no key-wrapping entry. The example files still carry the earlier model until they are updated.

$commentChangelog: Entries before v0.6 cite the pre-0.6 rule numbering, in which this profile's own rules ran M1 to M14 and its product rules continued the baseline's P-sequence. The v0.6 entry carries the mapping. Nothing was released under the old numbering, so no id is retired and none is held back from reuse; the no-reuse rule in decision 0011 starts from v0.6. The published v0.6 file is not treated as released either (decided in the revision that aligned the drafts with the use-case page), so the v0.7 entry renumbers ids and carries the v0.6 to v0.7 mapping. The v0.6 entry's mapping is kept as it was: it describes what the v0.6 file did.

changelog.summary: Initial draft. Derived from the interface disclosure baseline v0.3: adds product rules P3 and P4 and per-interface rules M1 to M12, and tightens inherited rule I9 by removing its withholdability.

changes.summary: Added 'scope' and narrowed the accepted lifecycle stages to implemented, configured and observed. An interface reporting 'intended' now fails I8, where under v0.1 it conformed. This is the first rule in either profile that discriminates on how the reported data was obtained rather than on what it says, and it is the reason the field exists: a migration plan built on cryptography a producer intends to implement is a plan built on an intention. See decision 0008.
Added 'objective.decisionOptions', stating the five actions the planner chooses between. The decision text itself is unchanged.

Re-pinned the base from v0.3 to v0.4. The base's v0.4 change was editorial and no inherited rule changed, but a pin names an exact version, so the derived profile is re-issued rather than silently following the base.

Added 'scope.orientation', declared here as 'both'. This profile reports present state and migration capability together, and under C12 that declaration obliges it to require the present-state counterpart of every capability attribute it requires. It already does, by inheritance: M1 to M3 require protocolVersionsSupported, keyExchangeSupported and authenticationSupported, and I2, I3 and I5 require the present-state attributes those are capabilities for. Declaring 'migration' instead would have been the inaccurate answer, since this profile does not report capability alone. See decision 0009.
Re-pinned the base from v0.4 to v0.5. No inherited rule changed.

Capability is now stated per cryptographic purpose. M10, M11 and M12 are replaced by the 'capabilityByPurpose' group rule M10, whose members M10.1 to M10.3 carry the status, the conditional blocker and the roadmap reference within each purpose entry. A document conforming to v0.3 carried one status for the interface and does not conform to v0.4, which requires one per purpose. This settles Q27: the ordinary position, key agreement done and identity proof not yet, was not expressible before. See decision 0010.

Coverage of M10 is the whole purpose vocabulary, not only the purposes named in scope.cryptographicPurposes. In-scope purposes owe the full attribute set; the rest owe a status and a blocker. This is what allows a profile to be staged without the earlier stage becoming a permanent floor.

Added cryptographicPurposeVocabulary and scope.cryptographicPurposes. The vocabulary is fixed by the methodology so that two profiles cannot mean different things by the same word; a sector profile widening it raises the mirror of Q35, which is unresolved.

Renumbered the product rules out of the baseline's P-space, under the first form of decision 0011. Superseded in v0.6, which renumbers the whole profile under the settled scheme; this entry is kept because it is what the v0.5 file did.

Re-pinned the base to v0.6, which adds P3 (subject identity) and P4 (completeness) and revises P2. Those requirements are inherited, so a document conforming to this profile now has to satisfy them too. The coverage statement this profile used to require itself is unchanged in substance and now arrives from the base.

Renumbered every rule this profile declares into its own local space under the settled decision 0011. Ids are local to the declaring profile and are cited as '<profileTag>#<ruleId>', so this profile numbers from I1, G1 and P1 without colliding with the baseline's I1 to I9 and P1 to P4, which it inherits unchanged. No requirement on any document changes and no rule changes meaning: rule ids appear in reports and claims, not in CBOMs. The override on the baseline's implementationPurl rule now names its target as 'interface-disclosure#I9', because a tightened rule keeps the id of the profile that introduced it. This mapping describes the v0.6 file as it was; the v0.7 entry carries the further renumbering.
Added 'profileTag'. Re-pinned the base to v0.7, which adds the same field and changes no rule.

Re-pinned the base to Interface Disclosure Baseline v0.8, which stops requiring channel attributes of a storage interface and adds keyWrapping for it (interface-disclosure#I12), moduleValidationScheme (#I10) and moduleValidationRef (#I11). Guarded I1 to I3 on the same condition, so that no capability attribute is required where its present-state counterpart is not. Added I6 (keyWrappingSupported), MUST on a storage interface. See decision 0022.

Module validation (moduleValidationScheme, moduleValidationRef) is not a rule of this profile. It is stated by the baseline v0.8 as interface-disclosure#I10 and #I11 and arrives here by inheritance. A document conforming to v0.6 does not conform to v0.7 until it states the validation of each interface's implementing module. Derived from the information cprofile.json carries under 'fips_compliance'. See decision 0022.

G1 now has nine members, one entry per cryptographic purpose. The interface-level rules enablementMethod, minimumProductVersion, negotiationControl and integrationConstraints become members G1.1, G1.2, G1.4 and G1.5, because their answer differs by purpose on one interface. negotiationStrategy is new (G1.3). capabilityStatus, blockedBy and roadmapRef become G1.6, G1.7 and G1.8. validatedModeAvailability is new (G1.9), SHOULD, guarded on capabilityStatus 'available'. A storage interface owes only the key-wrapping entry; any other interface owes the other six purposes. The purpose 'key-protection' is renamed 'key-wrapping'. See decision 0022.
Interface ids close up: providerLocation is I4 (was I6) and coexistence is I5 (was I7). I6 is the new keyWrappingSupported. Nothing is released under these ids (decision 0011).
This profile becomes the baseline depth of the PQC migration family (decisions 0019 and 0022). Its objective is unchanged; its rules change as the entries above record.
Implementation facts may be stated once on the providing implementation and inherited by the interfaces it provides (K9). Rules are evaluated on effective values; no rule changes.

Declared two proposed additions to the rules format, 'keyApplicability' on the group and 'inScopeOnly' on G1.1 to G1.5, which the group needs to say what the use-case page says. Neither is implemented by the published validator; see the notes on G1 and decision 0022.
